Bajaj Finance employs tens of thousands of staff—some reports mention over 53,000 employees—across sales, underwriting, technology, operations and support functions.[16][22] The company’s culture is described as intense and performance‑oriented, with high expectations around execution, but also as entrepreneurial and rewarding for those who thrive in such environments.[41][44] The large investment in technology and AI implies significant demand for skilled engineers and data scientists, offering opportunities for career growth but also requiring constant upskilling.  

Finally, as a systemically important NBFC, Bajaj Finance has responsibilities to regulators and to the broader financial system. Its adherence to high capital, liquidity and risk management standards reduces the probability of distress that could ripple across markets, particularly in light of the role NBFCs play in India’s credit intermediation.[12][50] The company’s continued dialogue with regulators on emerging issues such as digital lending, AI and data privacy will shape not only its own trajectory but also the evolution of the NBFC sector more broadly.  

## 7. Case Study: The FY2024–26 Cycle and the Q3 Dip / Q4 Rebound  

### 7.1 FY2024–25: Strong growth amid tightening conditions  

The period spanning FY2024 and FY2025 offers a useful case study of Bajaj Finance’s resilience in the face of regulatory tightening, rising interest rates and evolving credit conditions. In FY2024, the company delivered an outstanding performance: consolidated AUM grew 34% from ₹247,379 crore to ₹330,615 crore, PAT increased 26% from ₹11,508 crore to ₹14,451 crore, and RoA and RoE stood at 5.08% and 22.05% respectively. This performance was achieved despite the RBI’s mid‑year decision to increase risk weights on unsecured consumer loans, which raised capital requirements and put pressure on margins.  

The company responded by raising capital, strengthening its balance sheet, and continuing to invest in technology and new products. It added 14.5 million new customers in FY2024, bringing the total to 83.6 million, booked 36.2 million loans, and expanded its physical network and digital marketplaces. Asset quality remained robust, with GNPA at 0.85% and NNPA at 0.37%, better than pre‑COVID levels.  

In FY2025, growth remained strong but profit momentum moderated. AUM increased 26% to ₹416,661 crore, PAT grew 16% to ₹16,779 crore, and RoA and RoE, while still strong, moderated to 4.57% and 19.19%.[12][9] The company highlighted that it had invested heavily in digital and AI capabilities under its FinAI strategy and had launched new products in line with its Long‑Range Strategy, laying the foundation for future growth.[9][9]  

Analysts noted that while earnings growth in FY2025 was lower than in FY2024, it remained healthy at mid‑teens percentages, especially considering the high base and the regulatory backdrop. Axis Direct, for example, remarked that RoA and RoE were still strong and that the company had successfully raised capital, maintained a high CRAR, and navigated margin pressures with resilience.  

### 7.2 Q3 FY2025–26: Elevated provisions and a profit surprise  

The December quarter of FY2025–26 (Q3 FY26 in the company’s nomenclature) marked a deviation from the pattern of steady profit growth and triggered a degree of investor anxiety. Bajaj Finance reported a consolidated net profit of around ₹4,063–4,100 crore for the quarter, representing a 5–6% year‑on‑year decline, despite revenue growth of about 17–18%.[15][3]  

The primary driver of this profit decline was a sharp increase in provisions. Reuters reported that Bajaj Finance raised provisions by approximately ₹14.06 billion (₹1,406 crore) as it sought to bolster its balance sheet against global economic uncertainties and implemented a minimum loss‑given‑default threshold across various sectors.[3] The company indicated that this change in provisioning framework, combined with risk actions in parts of the MSME and auto book, resulted in higher credit costs for the quarter.[3][18]  

Investor presentations around the same time showed that GNPA and NNPA had risen to 1.59% and 0.77% respectively as of September 30, 2025, from sub‑1% levels earlier, although still low by sector standards.[18] Analysts such as those at Mangal Keshav described Q3 FY26 as a “stable” quarter operationally but noted one‑off losses or elevated provisions that weighed on headline profitability.  

Equity markets reacted to this surprise by marking down the stock, reflecting concerns that a structural deterioration in asset quality or a prolonged period of higher credit costs could compress earnings and challenge the high valuation multiple. Some commentary emphasised that Bajaj Finance faced tough competition for funding from banks and that its funding costs and credit costs were both under upward pressure, squeezing the profitability wedge.[34][32]  

At the same time, more constructive analysts argued that Bajaj Finance was taking the right steps by front‑loading provisions and tightening risk filters, even at the expense of short‑term earnings, and that its underlying growth engine remained intact. They pointed out that the company’s AUM and customer additions continued to grow at healthy rates and that early delinquencies showed signs of stabilising as risk actions took effect.  

### 7.3 Q4 FY2025–26: Rebound, AUM milestone and guidance  

The March quarter of FY2025–26 (Q4 FY26) provided a counterpoint to the gloom of Q3, as Bajaj Finance delivered a strong set of results that signalled resilience and renewed momentum. The company reported consolidated net profit of approximately ₹5,464–5,553 crore, representing a 22% year‑on‑year increase, driven by 20% growth in net interest income and 22% growth in AUM.[30]  

Crucially, the company announced that it had crossed the milestone of ₹5 lakh crore in AUM, ending the year at roughly ₹510,000 crore. In Q4 alone, AUM grew by about ₹25,500 crore—a record quarterly addition—and the company booked 12.9 million loans and added 3.93 million new customers. On a full‑year basis, it booked 52.5 million loans and added 17.5 million new customers, bringing the customer franchise to 119.3 million.  

In the Q4 FY26 earnings call, management described the quarter as “pretty strong across all key metrics” and expressed confidence that the company was returning to a trajectory of strong growth across AUM, profit, RoA and RoE. The company reiterated its long‑term business construct of delivering RoA of 4.3–4.7% and RoE of around 20–22%, and guided for profit growth of 20–24% for the upcoming year, assuming normalising credit costs and continued loan growth.  

Market reactions reflected this improved sentiment, with Bajaj Finance shares rising after the Q4 results announcement, even though the stock remained below its 52‑week high. Economic Times reports noted that the stock gained up to 4.2% following the Q4 print, aided by the announcement of special and final dividends and the crossing of the ₹5 lakh crore AUM mark.[30]  

Brokerage commentary after Q4 was generally positive. Prabhudas Lilladher, for instance, maintained a “Buy” rating, noting steady 22% AUM growth to ₹4,844.8 billion, traction in new verticals like cars, gold and microfinance, and expectations that credit costs, while elevated, would moderate by FY2027 as early‑stage delinquencies improved. Sector‑wide, diversified lenders such as Bajaj Finance and Cholamandalam were seen as driving optimism for the NBFC sector as FY2027 began, with most reporting loan growth above 20%.  

The Q3–Q4 episode thus illustrates Bajaj Finance’s willingness to absorb short‑term pain in the form of higher provisions in order to strengthen asset quality and risk buffers, and its capacity to regain growth momentum quickly thereafter. For long‑term observers, the key question is whether such episodes remain isolated and manageable or whether they foreshadow a structurally more volatile credit environment in which maintaining the historical combination of high growth and low NPAs becomes progressively more difficult.  

## 8. Synthesis: Durable Competitive Advantages and Key Watchpoints  

### 8.1 Sources of competitive advantage  

Drawing together the strands of this analysis, several sources of durable competitive advantage for Bajaj Finance become evident.  

First, its brand and distribution scale create formidable barriers to entry. The Bajaj name enjoys high recognition and trust, and Bajaj Finance’s presence across over 4,000 locations, nearly 2 lakh PoS outlets, and millions of merchants ensures that it is deeply embedded in India’s consumer and SME commerce fabric.[20] The EMI card and numerous PoS partnerships give it privileged access to customers at the point of purchase, a critical advantage in consumer lending and payments.  

Second, its customer franchise and data assets exert a flywheel effect. With over 110 million customers and a cross‑sell base approaching 70–75 million, Bajaj Finance can extract more value per customer through multiple products, while continuously refining risk and propensity models based on an immense repository of transaction and repayment data.[20] This granular data is a key input to its AI and analytics engines, creating a virtuous loop where more business leads to better models, which in turn enable more targeted and profitable business.  

Third, its diversified product portfolio and multi‑segment presence allow it to smooth earnings and optimise risk‑adjusted returns. By balancing high‑yield, short‑tenor unsecured consumer and SME loans with lower‑yield, longer‑tenor secured mortgages and auto loans, and by operating across urban, rural, MSME, commercial and housing segments, the company reduces reliance on any single product or cycle and can rotate growth towards segments with more favourable conditions.[12][40]  

Fourth, its funding and capital strength underpin resilience. The deposit‑taking license, AAA domestic credit ratings, diversified funding mix, high LCR and capital ratios well above regulatory minima mean that Bajaj Finance is less vulnerable to liquidity shocks and can continue growing even when market conditions tighten.[6][12] This contrasts with many smaller NBFCs that faced severe stress during past liquidity crunches and underscores why Bajaj Finance is often treated more like a bank in risk assessments.  

Fifth, its technology and AI capabilities are now central to its competitive positioning. The migration to cloud‑based core systems, the deployment of hundreds of AI agents, the proven ability of AI to originate large volumes of loans and generate personalised offers, and the commitment to make all products accessible via conversational AI interfaces represent a level of digital sophistication that few competitors have matched at similar scale.[21][48] This digital edge translates into faster time‑to‑yes for customers, lower operating costs, and more precise risk pricing, which can support both market share gains and margin preservation.
